rationale: Response B is stronger because it translates admin-managed fields into a metadata table plus JSONB rather than exposing runtime DDL, reducing migration, locking, injection, and data-loss risks while preserving dynamic forms and existing values. It also offers more coherent choices for opaque hashed refresh tokens with reuse detection, cursor pagination, soft deletion, last-admin protection, mass-assignment controls, and efficient set-based bulk updates. Response A is broader and its queued bulk-processing design is valuable, but allowing UI-driven creation and deletion of tables or columns is unnecessarily dangerous and operationally brittle. B still has weaknesses—deprecated or dubious sanitization-library advice, inconsistent wording around raw SQL, an optimistic one-week cadence, and tension between atomic bulk rollback and per-row errors—but its core data model and security architecture are more sound and actionable.
